result.summary: Apollodorus tells how Perseus, born to Danae, beheads Medusa, rescues Andromeda, and accidentally kills his grandfather Acrisius. The chapter then follows the descendants of Perseus down to Amphitryon, Alcmena and the birth, boyhood and early deeds of Hercules, ending with the oracle that sets him to serve Eurystheus.

scenes.title: Danae and the chest
scenes.summary: Warned that his grandson will kill him, Acrisius locks Danae away. She bears Perseus, and Acrisius casts them into the sea in a chest that lands at Seriphus.
scenes.stakes: Acrisius fears death at his grandson's hand; Danae and the infant Perseus face drowning.

scenes.title: Perseus wins Medusa's head
scenes.summary: Polydectes tricks Perseus into promising the Gorgon's head. With help from Hermes and Athena he gets the magic gear from the Phorcides and the nymphs and beheads Medusa.
scenes.stakes: Perseus risks being turned to stone by the Gorgons, and the mission is meant to get him killed.

scenes.title: Andromeda rescued in Ethiopia
scenes.summary: Perseus slays the sea monster and frees Andromeda, then turns Phineus and his fellow conspirators to stone.
scenes.stakes: Andromeda faces death by the monster; Perseus must keep the bargain and survive Phineus's plot.

scenes.title: Vengeance on Polydectes
scenes.summary: At Seriphus Perseus petrifies Polydectes and his friends, makes Dictys king, and returns the gear. Athena places the Gorgon's head on her shield.
scenes.stakes: Danae and Dictys are in danger from Polydectes.

scenes.title: Death of Acrisius
scenes.summary: Perseus's discus kills Acrisius at the games in Larissa, fulfilling the oracle. Perseus swaps Argos for Tiryns with Megapenthes.
scenes.stakes: Perseus must bear the guilt of killing his grandfather and give up his inheritance.

scenes.title: Descendants of Perseus
scenes.summary: The genealogy runs through Alcaeus, Mestor, Electryon and Sthenelus, and through Poseidon's descendants, the Teleboans. Hera delays Alcmena's labour so that Eurystheus is born first.

scenes.title: Cattle raid and Electryon's death
scenes.summary: The Taphians and Electryon's sons kill each other over the cattle. Amphitryon accidentally kills Electryon and is exiled to Thebes, where Creon asks him to deal with the vixen.
scenes.stakes: Amphitryon faces exile and blood guilt, and must win Alcmena by avenging her brothers.

scenes.title: The vixen and the Taphian war
scenes.summary: Cephalus's unfailing dog chases the uncatchable vixen and Zeus turns both to stone. Amphitryon then conquers the Taphian islands after Comaetho betrays her father.
scenes.stakes: Thebes loses a child every month to the vixen; Amphitryon must conquer the Taphians to win Alcmena.

scenes.title: Birth of Hercules
scenes.summary: Zeus takes Amphitryon's shape and lies with Alcmena, who bears Hercules and Iphicles. The infant Hercules strangles the serpents sent by Hera.
scenes.stakes: The infant Hercules faces death from Hera's serpents.

scenes.title: Youth and the Cithaeron lion
scenes.summary: Hercules is trained by famous teachers and kills Linus, but is acquitted. He kills the lion of Cithaeron while fathering children on Thespius's fifty daughters.
scenes.stakes: Hercules faces trial for murder and the danger of the lion.

scenes.title: War with the Minyans
scenes.summary: Hercules mutilates Erginus's heralds and defeats the Minyans. He wins Megara, and the gods arm him.
scenes.stakes: Thebes is threatened with Minyan conquest and renewed tribute.

scenes.title: Madness and the oracle
scenes.summary: Driven mad by Hera, Hercules burns his children. After purification he goes to Delphi, is named Hercules, and is told to serve Eurystheus for twelve years.
scenes.stakes: Hercules must atone for killing his children, and immortality depends on completing the labours.

alias_notes.explanation: Hercules's earlier name, before the Pythian priestess renamed him.
Collective name for the daughters of Phorcus: Enyo, Pephredo and Dino.

notable_quotes.reason: Explains the naming of Hercules, formerly Alcides, at Delphi.

analysis.text: Oracles and fate drive the chapter: Acrisius's attempt to escape prophecy fulfils it, and Hera's hostility shapes Hercules's life.
The chapter works as a genealogy linking Argive, Theban and Mycenaean royal houses to Perseus and Hercules, serving the claims of dynasties and cities.

legacy.text: The Perseus and Medusa story became a staple of Greek and later European art, and the Gorgon's head on Athena's shield (the aegis) became a standard image.
The film Clash of the Titans (1981) retells Perseus, Medusa and Andromeda, and was remade in 2010.

fun_facts.text: The Library, attributed to Apollodorus, is a prose handbook of Greek myth that often cites poets such as Hesiod and Pherecydes.

language_notes.text: Proetus is Acrisius's twin brother; the two famously quarrelled. The golden shower is Zeus's disguise to reach Danae.
"Man's estate" means adulthood; Perseus was now old enough to protect his mother from Polydectes.
Contributions toward a wedding gift (eranos) were a custom; Hippodamia's suitors had to win her by a chariot race, so horses were an apt demand.
"Stick at" means hesitate over; Perseus rashly boasts he would even fetch the Gorgon's head.
Kibisis: a pouch or wallet, here used to carry the severed head safely.
The cap of Hades made the wearer invisible; it belonged to the god of the dead.
Adamantine means unbreakable, made of the hardest substance; here describing a curved sickle.
A kibisis is a pouch or bag for carrying the head; "wallet" here means a traveler's bag, not a purse for money.
"Set out to be the prey" means she was exposed as a sacrifice, left for the monster to devour.
Ammon is the oracle of the god Ammon (Zeus Ammon) in Egypt, consulted here for a remedy to the disaster.
"To wife" is archaic for "as his wife"; the rescue is made a condition of marriage.
"Fain" means willing or eager; the Gorgon was keen to rival the goddess in beauty.
The oracle had told Acrisius that his daughter's son would kill him, which is why he fears Perseus.
The pentathlum (pentathlon) was a five-event contest; the quoit is the discus, a thrown disc.
Perses was held to be the ancestor of the Persians, a Greek legend explaining the people's name by linking them to Perseus.
Teleboans is explained by a Greek pun: 'tele' means 'far', so the name means 'those who went far'.
The golden hair made Pterelaus immortal as long as it stayed in place; in the usual story it is later plucked out and he dies.
The Ilithyias are the goddesses of childbirth, who could hasten or delay a delivery.
Kine is an old plural for cows; here it means cattle.
'Stood on their defence' means the sons resisted the raiders and fought to protect the cattle.
The oath to keep Alcmena a virgin means Amphitryon must not marry or sleep with her until Electryon returns.
'Purified' refers to ritual cleansing from the pollution of bloodshed, even when the killing was accidental.
The Cadmea was the citadel of Thebes, named after its founder Cadmus.
"The brute" is the Teumessian vixen, a monstrous fox sent to ravage Thebes; "exposed" means left out to be devoured.
"Betook him to" is archaic for "went to"; "Teleboan spoils" are the plunder expected from the war against the Taphians/Teleboans.
The paradox of a dog that always catches what it chases against a fox that can never be caught is resolved by Zeus petrifying both.
"To wit" is an archaic formula meaning "namely", introducing the list of allies.
Pterelaus's golden hair made him immortal or invulnerable, so cutting it off let him die; Comaetho's betrayal is the key to the conquest.
Zeus lengthens the night to three times its normal length, which explains Hercules' later epithet of being "of the triple night" in some accounts.
Tiresias is the famous blind Theban seer, who explains the divine deception.
Pherecydes was a Greek mythographer; the author offers his variant account of the serpents as a test of paternity.
To "fence" means to fight with swords; Castor, one of the Dioscuri, was a famed warrior.
Rhadamanthys was a legendary just lawgiver, later a judge of the dead; his law is cited as precedent for self-defence.
A cubit is an ancient measure of about 18 inches, so four cubits is roughly six feet.
This translation spells the god's name Zeus here, though other passages use Jove; the father of Hercules is the king of the gods.
"Kine" is an archaic plural for cattle; "harried" means raided or plagued.
"Bedded one of his daughters with him" means Thespius sent a different daughter to sleep with Hercules each night.
"Outraged" here means physically abused or mutilated, not merely offended.
The Pythian priestess was the oracle of Apollo at Delphi; the name Hercules means roughly "glory of Hera," ironic given her hostility.

context_notes.text: Acrisius was king of Argos; oracles at Delphi were consulted for guidance and their answers were usually fulfilled.
The Phorcides, also called the Graiai, were Gorgon sisters who shared a single eye and tooth and knew the road to the nymphs.
Pegasus and Chrysaor spring from Medusa's neck; Poseidon was their father. Chrysaor fathered the monster Geryon, later killed by Heracles.
The Nereids are sea nymphs, daughters of Nereus. Poseidon, god of the sea, often punishes those who offend sea powers.
Hermes lent Perseus the winged sandals and other gear, so returning them closes the borrowing.
Athena's shield bearing the Gorgon's head is her aegis, which terrifies enemies.
Tiryns and Argos were neighboring cities in the Argolid; Megapenthes was a cousin through Proetus, Acrisius's brother.
Poseidon, god of the sea, fathered many heroes and tribes; the Echinadian Islands lie off western Greece.
Hera was Zeus's wife and goddess of marriage. She persecuted Hercules, son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmena.
Atreus and Thyestes, sons of Pelops, were later bitter rivals and fathers of Agamemnon and Aegisthus respectively.
Cephalus of Athens and his wife Procris appear in other myths; Minos, king of Crete, had given her the hunting dog.
Amphitryon kills Comaetho despite her help, a mark of how the story treats betrayal even when it benefits the victor.
Hercules and Iphicles are half-brothers: twins in some versions, one divine and one mortal son.
Hera, wife of Zeus, persecutes Hercules throughout his life because he is the child of her husband's affair.
Linus, a legendary musician, was Hercules' music teacher; the story says he struck the pupil, who retaliated with the lyre.
Erginus was king of the Minyans of Orchomenus, a city that dominated Thebes until Hercules' intervention.
Gifts from gods equip Hercules: a sword, bow, breastplate and robe, while his club he cut himself at Nemea.
Eurystheus, king of Tiryns, imposes the labours; Hera's hostility lies behind Hercules' subjection to him.

literary_notes.text: The oracle's prophecy sets the story's fate in motion, signalling that Acrisius's attempts to avoid death will fail.
Acrisius's attempt to prevent the prophecy by imprisoning Danae sets in motion the events that fulfil it.
The shared eye and tooth give a vivid, grotesque picture of the sisters and make Perseus's theft easy to grasp.
The reflecting shield stands for indirect, careful approach: Perseus defeats a deadly gaze by never meeting it directly.
Polydectes' men are frozen mid-gesture, a grim fitting punishment: those who plotted against Perseus's mother become permanent statues.
Acrisius's flight from the oracle only leads him to the place where it will be fulfilled.
A chance throw of the discus kills Acrisius, fulfilling the oracle he fled and showing the inevitability of fate.
Zeus's own declaration is turned against his son: his boast gives Hera the chance to hand the throne to Eurystheus instead.
A harmless throw at an animal accidentally kills the king, whom Amphitryon had just served by recovering the cattle.
The statement that the vixen cannot be caught hints at a paradox that will need a clever or divine solution.
Two unstoppable forces meet, and the only resolution is divine intervention that freezes both, ending the contradiction.
A hero's success depends on a woman's betrayal of her family through desire, a recurring pattern in Greek myth.
The infant's easy victory over the serpents anticipates his later heroic labors and his strength against Hera's hostility.
Fiery eyes and giant stature mark Hercules as semi-divine, showing his heroic nature through physical description.
Hercules is deceived about his bedfellow, so he unknowingly fathers children on all fifty sisters.
Wearing the lion's skin as a helmet becomes his emblem, displaying conquered ferocity and his heroic identity.
Hera's induced madness and the exile that follows set up the labours as atonement.
The promise of immortality after the tasks looks ahead to Hercules' eventual apotheosis.
